text: Abstract—Indian agriculture remains fundamentally dependent on the southwest monsoon, rendering rural livelihoods highly vulnerable to the climate anomalies triggered by the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Although historical atmospheric investigations have established qualitative associations between warm equatorial Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies and all-India monsoon deficits, empirical assessments that quantify the resulting macroeconomic damage to crop output across diverse state-level agro-climatic zones in real economic currency remain sparse. In this paper, we construct an official, reproducible panel dataset comprising 385 complete state-years across 28 Indian states spanning FY 2011–12 through FY 2024–25. The dataset synchronizes India Meteorological Department (IMD) daily gridded precipitation (0.25° × 0.25°) and daily minimum/maximum temperature (1.0° × 1.0°) products with NOAA Climate Prediction Center Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) and official Reserve Bank of India (RBI) / National Statistical Office (NSO) Crop Gross State Value Added (GSVA) at constant 2011–12 prices (₹ crore). We deploy and benchmark five machine learning regression families under a strict chronological time-aware partitioning scheme (training on FY 2011–12 to 2019–20, held-out testing on FY 2020–21 to 2023–24) to eliminate temporal lookahead bias: Linear Regression (OLS with state fixed-effects), Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, and Extra Trees Regressor. The Extra Trees ensemble achieved superior empirical generalization on the held-out test partition, recording a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 15.68 ₹ crore, a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 12.19 ₹ crore, a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.5224, and a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 11.23%, outperforming linear baseline specifications by 10.3% in RMSE. Gini feature importance decomposition indicates that compound thermal stress (mean temperature, 61.44%) and seasonal rainfall (27.90%) serve as primary proximate drivers of agricultural value added, while ONI (10.66%) functions as an overarching atmospheric phase shifter. Comprehensive scenario stress-testing reveals acute spatial vulnerability divergence: rainfed agricultural states (Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat) suffer projected crop GSVA contractions between 14.6% and 17.9% under severe El Niño (+2.0°C) conditions, whereas canal-irrigated northern plains (Punjab, Haryana) maintain high economic resilience (<2.5% contraction). These findings provide an empirical, data-driven framework for targeted fiscal contingency allocations, parametric crop insurance calibration, and regional irrigation planning.

text: Agriculture constitutes the foundation of the Indian socio-economic structure, employing approximately 54 percent of the national workforce and generating roughly 18 percent of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) [1], [2]. The sector is intrinsically intertwined with the June-to-September southwest monsoon, which supplies more than 70 percent of India's total annual precipitation [3]. Because less than 52 percent of the net sown area in India benefits from assured perennial irrigation facilities, inter-annual monsoon fluctuations propagate directly into agricultural production cycles, causing sharp oscillations in kharif crop sowing acreage, harvest yields, agricultural wholesale price indices, and overall rural purchasing power [4].

    <w:t>Agriculture constitutes the foundation of the Indian socio-economic structure, employing approximately 54 percent of the national workforce and generating roughly 18 percent of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) [1], [2]. The sector is intrinsically intertwined with the June-to-September southwest monsoon, which supplies more than 70 percent of India's total annual precipitation [3].   </w:r>

text: The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)—manifested through periodic positive sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean—represents the single most dominant global driver of Indian summer monsoon variability [5], [6]. Canonical research over recent decades has documented that warm ENSO phases disrupt the tropical atmospheric Walker circulation, displacing deep tropical convection eastward and inducing widespread anomalous descending motion over the South Asian landmass [7], [8]. This subsidence dampens moisture convergence, suppresses deep convective cloud formation, and frequently leads to severe, widespread seasonal drought [9]. Historically, six out of the ten most devastating all-India droughts of the past century—including the benchmark agricultural crisis years of 1987, 2002, 2004, 2009, 2014, 2015, and 2023—coincided directly with positive tropical Pacific SST anomalies [10], [11].

text: Despite extensive atmospheric documentation of the ENSO-monsoon relationship, existing agricultural climate-impact literature in India exhibits four fundamental limitations: First, the overwhelming majority of existing studies focus on all-India or meteorological sub-divisional rainfall totals measured in physical millimeters or aggregate grain harvest volume measured in metric tons [12], [13]. While physical harvest metrics are informative, they fail to reflect the realized economic value added at constant financial prices. Physical volume does not capture crop-mix substitution, post-harvest distress selling, or price-adjusted macroeconomic contributions captured in official national economic accounts [14]. Second, national aggregates mask acute regional and state-level agro-climatic divergence. India exhibits vast geographical heterogeneity in agrarian infrastructure: highly developed, tubewell-dense states in the northern Indo-Gangetic plains (such as Punjab and Haryana) possess irrigation cover exceeding 95 percent, allowing them to buffer monsoon deficits through intensive groundwater extraction. In contrast, states situated across the semi-arid central and peninsular Deccan plateau (such as Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, and Rajasthan) rely on rainfed cultivation for 60 to 82 percent of their cropped area, rendering them acutely vulnerable to abrupt economic collapse during warm ENSO years [15], [16]. Third, prevailing statistical investigations commonly rely on classical ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regressions, structural equation modeling, or subjective analytic hierarchy process (AHP) index weighting [17], [18]. Such approaches are incapable of modeling complex, non-linear agro-climatic thresholds, such as asymmetric thermal crop stress or compound drought-heat wave interactions [19]. Fourth, when modern machine learning techniques have been applied to agricultural time-series panels, authors frequently utilize randomized k-fold cross-validation. This methodology inadvertently causes temporal data leakage between past and future records, yielding artificially inflated accuracy scores that fail to hold in operational predictive deployment [20].

text: To overcome these critical empirical limitations, this study presents a rigorous, reproducible machine learning panel investigation evaluating the quantitative teleconnection between El Niño climate anomalies and Crop Gross State Value Added (GSVA) across 28 Indian states over 14 consecutive financial years (FY 2011–12 to FY 2024–25). The major contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 1) We construct an official, leak-free panel dataset comprising 385 complete state-years that harmonizes India Meteorological Department (IMD) high-resolution gridded daily rainfall (0.25° × 0.25°) and temperature (1.0° × 1.0°) records with NOAA CPC Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) values and official RBI/NSO Crop GSVA at constant 2011–12 prices. 2) We establish a strict chronological time-aware validation framework (training on FY 2011–12 to 2019–20, held-out testing on FY 2020–21 to 2023–24) to evaluate five distinct regression model families (Linear Regression OLS, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, and Extra Trees Regressor) without temporal lookahead bias. 3) We quantify the relative explanatory power of individual climate drivers via tree-based Gini feature importance decomposition, revealing the decisive role of thermal anomalies alongside precipitation deficits. 4) We execute scenario-based simulation stress-tests projecting state-level crop GSVA vulnerability and economic contraction under neutral, moderate (+1.0°C), and strong (+2.0°C) El Niño events, providing an empirical roadmap for targeted drought relief and crop-insurance budgeting.

xmlns:wne="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2006/wordml" xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape" w14:paraId="2A8B03F4" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00C0358A" w:rsidRDefault="00000000">
  <w:pPr>
    <w:spacing w:after="100"/>
    <w:ind w:firstLine="288"/>
    <w:jc w:val="both"/>
  </w:pPr>
  <w:r>
    <w:t xml:space="preserve">To overcome these critical empirical limitations, this study presents a rigorous, reproducible machine learning panel investigation evaluating the quantitative teleconnection between El Niño climate anomalies and Crop Gross State Value Added (GSVA) across 28 Indian states over 14 consecutive financial years (FY 2011–12 to FY 2024–25). The major contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 1) We construct an official, leak-free panel dataset comprising 385 complete state-years that harmonizes India Meteorological Department (IMD) high-resolution gridded daily rainfall (0.25° × 0.25°) and temperature (1.0° × 1.0°) records with NOAA CPC Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) values and official RBI/NSO Crop GSVA at constant 2011–12 prices. 2) We establish a strict chronological time-aware validation framework (training on FY 2011–12 to 2019–20, held-out testing on FY 2020–21 to 2023–24) to evaluate five distinct regression model families (Linear Regression OLS, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, </w:t>
  </w:r>
  <w:proofErr w:type="spellStart"/>
  <w:r>
    <w:t>XGBoost</w:t>
  </w:r>
  <w:proofErr w:type="spellEnd"/>
  <w:r>
    <w:t>, and Extra Trees Regressor) without temporal lookahead bias. 3) We quantify the relative explanatory power of individual climate drivers via tree-based Gini feature importance decomposition, revealing the decisive role of thermal anomalies alongside precipitation deficits. 4) We execute scenario-based simulation stress-tests projecting state-level crop GSVA vulnerability and economic contraction under neutral, moderate (+1.0°C), and strong (+2.0°C) El Niño events, providing an empirical roadmap for targeted drought relief and crop-insurance budgeting.</w:t>
  </w:r>
</w:p>

text: Gross State Value Added (GSVA) for the crop sub-sector at constant 2011–12 prices (measured in ₹ crore) represents the net monetary value of all agricultural crops produced within a state, after deducting intermediate consumption (seeds, fertilizers, fuel, electricity, and pesticides). Formulated by the National Statistical Office (NSO) and published by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), this metric eliminates inflationary price distortions and captures the true real purchasing power generated by the agricultural sector, providing an optimal target for macroeconomic climate modeling.

    <w:t>A.  ENSO Dynamics and Indian Summer Monsoon Teleconnections</w:t>
  </w:r>

text: The fundamental physics of ENSO teleconnections over the Indian subcontinent were first mathematically outlined by Walker and later formalized by Rasmusson and Carpenter [7], who established that positive SST anomalies in the central Pacific correlate with widespread rainfall deficits over India. In seminal contributions, Kumar et al. [5], [6] observed that while historically over 60 percent of severe droughts occurred during El Niño years, the correlation has displayed decadal non-stationarity since the late 1980s. Kumar et al. [5] demonstrated that this weakening was driven by a southeastward shift in tropical Pacific convective heating, which reduced the subsidence anomaly over central India. Gadgil et al. [8] subsequently emphasized the modulating role of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD): warm El Niño events accompanied by positive IOD phases (such as 1997) frequently avoid catastrophic drought, whereas El Niño events occurring with neutral or negative IOD phases (such as 2002 and 2009) almost inevitably trigger severe country-wide monsoon failure. Recent work by van Oldenborgh et al. [21] further established that background anthropogenic global warming necessitates tracking detrended or relative oceanic indices to prevent spurious inflation of El Niño classifications.

text: In agricultural economics, Birthal et al. [22] conducted extensive econometric panel regressions across Indian districts, determining that an unmitigated 1°C increase in mean temperature reduces net agricultural revenue by 4.2 to 6.8 percent. Mishra and Singh [10] reviewed drought concepts across South Asia, highlighting that meteorological droughts rapidly transition into agricultural and socioeconomic crises when soil moisture depletion intersects with crop reproductive phenology. Swami and Parthasarathy [16] built an indicator-based vulnerability framework for Maharashtra districts across a 50-year horizon (1966–2015), showing that agricultural dependence and irrigation deficits exacerbate drought severity. Most recently, Deshmukh et al. [15] developed an exploratory district-level composite vulnerability index for 34 Maharashtra districts using principal component analysis (PCA) with sign-safe absolute loadings and K-Means clustering (K=3), validating their index against official state government drought declarations in 2018, 2023, and 2026. While informative, indicator-weighting schemes do not directly predict monetary economic output, highlighting the need for supervised machine learning regression.

text: Supervised learning algorithms have rapidly gained prominence for capturing high-dimensional, non-linear relationships in environmental modeling. Random Forest [23] and Gradient Boosted Decision Trees [24] have consistently surpassed classical autoregressive moving average (ARIMA) and multi-linear specifications in crop yield forecasting across North America and East Asia [25]. Chen and Guestrin [26] developed XGBoost, demonstrating its resilience to tabular data noise through second-order gradient expansion and column subsampling. In India, Saha et al. [18] applied fuzzy AHP and machine learning to map drought risk in Odisha, while Balaganesh et al. [19] utilized regression trees for Tamil Nadu. However, existing studies have predominantly relied on random cross-validation splits, which leak chronological trends. Our framework addresses this challenge through strict time-aware evaluation.

text: The study area covers the Republic of India across its 28 constituent states. Union Territories (such as Delhi, Chandigarh, Puducherry, and Ladakh) were excluded because their agricultural economies are negligible and official NSO crop-specific GSVA accounts are discontinuous. The temporal modeling window spans 14 consecutive financial years, from FY 2011–12 (commencing 1 April 2011) through FY 2024–25 (ending 31 March 2025).

text: Climate telemetry was derived from India Meteorological Department (IMD) high-resolution gridded daily products: the 0.25° × 0.25° daily rainfall dataset [27] and the 1.0° × 1.0° daily maximum and minimum temperature datasets [28]. To construct a consistent panel without boundary-interpolation artifacts, climate variables for each state were extracted from the nearest IMD grid cell corresponding to verified state representative centroid coordinates [29]. Annual rainfall (in millimeters) was computed by summing daily precipitation across the financial year, while annual mean temperature was computed by averaging daily minimum and maximum readings.

text: The El Niño index utilized is the NOAA Climate Prediction Center Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), derived from the 3-month running mean of ERSST.v5 sea surface temperature anomalies in the central-eastern equatorial Pacific Niño 3.4 region (5°N–5°S, 120°W–170°W) [30]. The financial-year ONI value was calculated as the unweighted mean of the ten complete overlapping 3-month seasons falling within the financial year (from AMJ through JFM).

text: The economic target is official Crop GSVA at constant 2011–12 prices (₹ crore), extracted from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Handbook of Statistics on Indian States and verified against MoSPI State Domestic Product accounts [13]. Of 392 potential state-year pairs (28 states × 14 years), 385 contain fully verified official entries. Seven missing values (Goa FY 2024–25; Gujarat FY 2023–24 and 2024–25; and Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim FY 2024–25) were excluded from training rather than imputed, ensuring zero synthetic data leakage. text: In time-series panel data, conventional random k-fold cross-validation allows past observations to be predicted using future data points, causing severe lookahead leakage. To guarantee realistic forecasting validity, we partition the 14-year panel chronologically. Financial years 2011–12 through 2019–20 (comprising 110 state-year records across the 28 states) constitute the training partition. Financial years 2020–21 through 2023–24 (comprising 40 held-out state-year records) form the untouched test partition. Models are trained exclusively on historical data and tested on future unseen years.

text: We implement and benchmark five distinct model families: 1) Linear Regression (OLS Baseline): Formulated with one-hot state dummy fixed-effects in (1) to capture time-invariant state characteristics (such as geographical landmass, baseline soil fertility, and irrigation canal networks). 2) Random Forest Regressor: An ensemble of B = 150 bagged decision trees that recursively partition the feature space to minimize variance, defined in (2). 3) Extra Trees Regressor (Extremely Randomized Trees): An ensemble that draws cut-point thresholds completely at random for each candidate feature rather than searching for optimal split thresholds [31], providing maximum regularization against noisy climate anomalies. 4) Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBM): Sequential boosting fitting decision trees to the negative gradient of the squared error loss function via gradient descent, defined in (3). 5) XGBoost Regressor: Scalable extreme gradient boosted tree implementation incorporating second-order Taylor expansions and explicit L1/L2 leaf weight regularization penalties, defined in (4).

text: Comprehensive benchmarking metrics across all five machine learning regressors on the held-out test dataset (FY 2020–21 through FY 2023–24) are synthesized in TABLE III and illustrated in Fig. 3. The Extra Trees Regressor achieved superior predictive generalization across all evaluation criteria, recording an RMSE of 15.68 ₹ crore, an MAE of 12.19 ₹ crore, an R² of 0.5224, and a MAPE of 11.23%.

text: Fig. 2 portrays the 40-year teleconnective trajectory of Indian summer monsoon rainfall departures against the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) from 1982 through 2024. During canonical El Niño episodes (1987, 2002, 2009, 2014, 2015, and 2023), all-India precipitation dropped sharply below the IMD deficient threshold of −10%, reaching severe deficits of −19.2% in 2002 and −21.8% in 2009. The corresponding crop GSVA figures across rainfed states exhibited immediate, concurrent economic contractions.

text: Gini feature importance decomposition summarized in TABLE IV and visualized in Fig. 4 reveals that annual mean temperature is the single most influential proximate driver of crop value added, accounting for 61.44% of total variance in the Extra Trees model. Cumulative rainfall accounts for 27.90%, while ONI accounts for 10.66%. This indicates that while El Niño shifts Pacific sea surface temperatures, its physical damage to Indian crops manifests primarily as compound thermal stress and seasonal precipitation deficits.

    <w:jc w:val="both"/>
  </w:pPr>
  <w:r>
    <w:t>Gini feature importance decomposition summarized in TABLE IV and visualized in Fig. 4 reveals that annual mean temperature is the single most influential proximate driver of crop value added, accounting for 61.44% of total variance in the Extra Trees model. Cumulative rainfall accounts for 27.90%, while ONI accounts for 10.66%. This indicates that while El Niño shifts Pacific sea surface temperatures, its physical damage to Indian crops manifests primarily as compound thermal stress and seasonal precipitation deficits.</w:t>

</w:p>

text: State-level scenario simulations depicted in TABLE V and Fig. 6 elucidate sharp geographical vulnerability disparities: under an extreme El Niño shock (+2.0°C ONI anomaly), rainfed agricultural states experience acute contractions: Rajasthan (−17.9%), Madhya Pradesh (−15.8%), Gujarat (−15.1%), and Maharashtra (−14.6%). In contrast, canal-irrigated states in the northern Indo-Gangetic basin exhibit substantial economic resilience: Punjab (−2.3%) and Haryana (−3.1%).

text: As shown in TABLE III, tree ensemble architectures substantially outperform the classical Linear Regression baseline (RMSE = 17.49 ₹ crore, R² = 0.4058). The Extra Trees algorithm delivers a 10.3% reduction in RMSE over OLS. By randomizing cut-point thresholds across candidate features, Extra Trees avoids co-adaptation to idiosyncratic climate spikes in the training set, preventing the overfitting observed in standard XGBoost (RMSE = 19.09 ₹ crore).

text: The results in TABLE V and Fig. 6 confirm that agrarian climate vulnerability is primarily mediated by irrigation infrastructure. In states where canal networks and tubewell electrification provide perennial water security, farmers buffer rainfall deficits by intensifying groundwater pumping, sustaining crop GSVA even during deficient monsoons. Conversely, in the rainfed Deccan trap and central plateaus, groundwater reserves are limited, so monsoon failure triggers immediate harvest destruction and economic distress.

text: Several methodological limitations must be stated explicitly. First, climate variables were extracted from the nearest IMD grid cell to documented state representative centroid coordinates rather than spatial area-weighted polygon integrals. While representative centroids avoid boundary distortion, coastal states with elongated geography (such as Goa and Kerala) may experience localized precipitation divergence.

text: This study developed a machine learning panel assessment evaluating the impact of El Niño climate teleconnections on Crop Gross State Value Added across 28 Indian states over a 14-year horizon (FY 2011–12 to FY 2024–25). Under strict chronological time-aware partitioning, the Extra Trees Regressor established benchmark generalization (RMSE = 15.68 ₹ crore, R² = 0.5224), outperforming linear and boosting baselines. The empirical findings substantiate that compound thermal stress and rainfall deficits drive crop value contractions, with rainfed central and western states suffering losses of up to 17.9% under severe El Niño conditions.

text: These empirical results translate into four concrete policy recommendations: 1) Predictive Early-Warning Triggering: Central and state disaster management authorities should utilize operational seasonal ONI forecasts to trigger preemptive fiscal credit guarantees and agricultural relief funds ahead of the kharif sowing window, rather than waiting for post-harvest loss declarations. 2) Parametric Crop Insurance Reform: The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) should integrate thermal anomaly thresholds alongside rainfall indices, reflecting the reality that temperature stress carries more than double the explanatory importance of rainfall in crop value losses. 3) Climate-Resilient Cropping Architecture: State agricultural extension agencies in high-vulnerability regions (Marathwada, Vidarbha, Bundelkhand, and western Rajasthan) must accelerate crop diversification away from water-intensive sugarcane and paddy toward drought-tolerant coarse cereals, millets, and pulses. 4) Decentralized Solar Micro-Irrigation: Public capital expenditures should prioritize decentralized farm-pond recharge networks and solar-powered micro-drip irrigation in rainfed states to bridge the resilience gap between central India and the irrigated northern plains.
